items.title: Residents warned to brace for the worst as Canada wildfire rages out of control
body: 'It's going crazy': Eyewitnesses capture forest fires raging across British Columbia

A state of emergency has been declared after thousands of people were forced to flee their homes as a fast-moving wildfire spread rapidly in western Canada, doubling in size since it was first detected on Friday.
Police said one person has died in the Bald Range fire, which is burning across 53 sq miles (136 sq km) in Summerland and other areas of British Columbia, according to the BC Wildfire Service.
"We have to brace ourselves for the worst," Summerland Mayor Doug Holmes told Reuters. The Summerland area has been forced to evacuate along with thousands of others in nearby communities.
Officials said flames were so high they had created their own weather systems, which creates lightning.
Image source, ReutersImage caption, The Bald Range wildfire burns, as seen from a vehicle, northwest of Summerland, British Columbia, Canada

Canadian police said on Sunday an 80-year-old woman from Meadow Valley, north-west of Summerland, had died suddenly while attempting to flee her home along with a member of her family. "Police believe her death to be a result of the wildfire," police said in a statement.
Keegan Radomski who lives in Summerland said she evacuated her home just moments before the fire reached her property.
In a video she shared with the BBC, burning tree tops are seen just over the hill beyond the road where Radomski made her escape.
"This is right by our house," she said in the video, her voice trembling.

Radomski said she has been unable to return since she fled with seven others on Friday. Now they're anxiously waiting on word whether they will still have a home to return to. She said some neighbours who stayed behind have reported many homes on their street burned down.
"There are homes that have been confirmed gone, and a lot are in the area near our home. So, we're pretty scared," she said. "The uncertainty is scary."

items.title: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan appears in court after extradition
body: Suspected crime boss Daniel Kinahan, one of the world's most wanted men, has appeared before a Dublin court after being extradited from Dubai.
He has been charged with directing the activities of a criminal organisation between 18 October 2015 and 6 April 2017.
An Irish government jet carrying the 49-year-old landed in Dublin after 18:00 local time. He was arrested and charged upon his arrival.
Following a 13-minute non-jury hearing at the Special Criminal Court, he was remanded in custody until 5 October.
Kinahan was arrested in the United Arab Emirates (UAE) in April. He appealed the extradition order over the past few months but his attempts were unsuccessful.

The National Crime Agency (NCA) has previously said that the Kinahan cartel has been responsible for importing tonnes of drugs and firearms around the world and has also been linked to more than a dozen gangland murders.
Kinahan was not only wanted by the authorities in Ireland - the US Treasury Department once described the Kinahan cartel as one of the most dangerous in the world.
Image source, PA MediaImage caption, Daniel Kinahan arrived into Casement Aerodrome in Baldonnel, Dublin on the government jet on Sunday evening
The US government imposed sanctions on Kinahan in April 2022 after identifying him and other members of his family as leaders of the Kinahan organised crime cartel.
He fought attempts to extradite him back to his native country, where the Kinahan cartel was involved in a long-running gangland feud that claimed 18 lives.
A large-scale security operation was in place ahead of Sunday's hearing.
Ahead of the extradition, the Irish Prison Service bought a bulletproof and bombproof van which can be used to escort prisoners who are considered high-risk.

items.title: Israel rejects Trump's 15-point plan for Gaza, Netanyahu says
body: Trump's Board of Peace said last month it had reached an agreement for the "complete disarmament" of Hamas and other armed groups in Gaza.
But Hamas said handing over its heavy weapons was contingent on Israel ending "all forms of aggression" and withdrawing its forces from Gaza.
On Sunday, a senior Board of Peace official insisted the US-backed peace plan for the territory remained the only way forward.
Israel has continued to carry out strikes on Gaza since agreeing to an initial ceasefire in the territory last October.
"Israel rejects the 15-point document," Netanyahu said at a cabinet meeting on Sunday.
The Israeli military "will not carry out any withdrawal until Hamas is genuinely disarmed and will continue to thwart threats against our forces and our citizens", he added.
A Hamas official told the BBC on Sunday the group "reaffirms it commitment" to the agreement and it was ready "to engage seriously and responsibly in implementing" the 15-point plan.
They called on mediators to ensure "that all parties comply with what has been agreed".
Israel's rejection signals another blow for Trump's Gaza peace plan which was announced in September last year.
The plan included the creation of the Board of Peace to oversee the agreement's implementation, as well as the disarmament of Hamas, withdrawal of Israeli troops and reconstruction of Gaza.
Published31 JulyNetanyahu's statement does not come as a surprise.
But he has taken some time to make it, perhaps reflecting the difficult position the Israeli leader is in.

items.title: Evidence that South African special forces murdered top detective shared with BBC
body: Senior police detective Frans Mathipa had been fighting for four months to gain access to a crucial piece of information in the case he was working on. Finally, he was told, it was going to come his way.
But he feared his pursuit of it could cost him his life.
Two days later, his car was found overturned - he had been shot dead while driving.

Now seven members of South Africa's special forces, and one military police officer, have been charged with murdering Lt Col Mathipa, a highly respected officer, in August 2023. They deny the charges.

There has been no date scheduled for their trial, and there are concerns it will never go ahead, because three of the men charged with his murder have refused to comply with a court order revoking their bail. They are still working for the army's special forces, and one of them has been promoted.
Image source, South African policeImage caption, Mathipa was killed as he was driving home along a motorway outside Pretoria
The BBC World Service has been given exclusive access to the prosecution case against all the men.
The case has caused consternation in one of Africa's most robust democracies, with fears the country's military is significantly overreaching its mandate.
We asked the South African army whether it was responsible for Mathipa's killing. It did not respond.

Several hundred pages of secret police and court documents, shared with the BBC, set out the evidence suggesting special forces killed Mathipa - who worked for an elite police unit known as "The Hawks".

We have also interviewed key sources in the police investigation - South Africa's former head of counter-terrorism in The Hawks; Mathipa's commanding officer; and Mathipa's family - to build the most comprehensive public account of the events leading up to the detective's death.
It presents a compelling case that South Africa's special forces are responsible for his murder.

items.title: Drones spotted over German base days after Leipzig bomb incident
body: Germany's armed forces (Bundeswehr) confirmed they were seen on Thursday evening at a base in Mechernich, near Bonn, reportedly housing components for US-made Patriot air-defence systems.
A spokeswoman for the Bundeswehr Joint Force Command said military police were deployed to the site before the matter was handed over to local police.

It is the latest instance of drones being spotted near military bases or airports in European nations supporting Ukraine in its war with Russia, on which suspicion has fallen. Moscow has consistently denied any involvement.
German Interior Minister Alexander Dobrindt told newspaper Bild on Sunday that Germany had become a regular target of "destabilising" attacks.
"We're not at war, but we are the daily target of hybrid warfare," he said.

Germany is currently investigating how a drone laden with explosives was able to reach a runway at Leipzig/Halle airport, which is used by Nato, the Germany military and serves as a base for Ukraine's Antonov Airlines.
The Bundeswehr declined to comment on the ongoing investigation when asked by the BBC on Sunday about the suspected origins of the drones spotted above Mechernich.
The local police force has been contacted for comment.
German media reports that the base has a storage facility for equipment ​and spare parts used to maintain the Patriot missile batteries.
The air-defence systems have become crucial to Ukraine's ability to intercept Russian ballistic missiles since Moscow's full-scale invasion began in 2022.
However, President Volodymyr Zelensky this week pleaded to allies for further supplies, warning that Ukraine was running out of interceptor missiles.
After initially offering Ukraine license to make Patriots in early July, US President Donald Trump last week denied any such agreement.

items.title: Ancient Roman shipwreck discovered off Sicily coast
body: Watch: Shipwreck discovered piled high with ancient pottery
Italian divers have discovered an ancient Roman shipwreck off the coast of Sicily, believed to be more than 2,000 years old.
The vessel was found piled high with hundreds of well-preserved containers, which were used to transport goods such as wine and olive oil.
Italy's Culture Minister Alessandro Giuli hailed the wreck as "one of the most important underwater archaeological discoveries of recent years".
Specialist police divers found the ship around 46m (150ft) deep, after a tip-off from fishermen. The wreckage is 21m (69ft) long and 6m (20ft) wide, according to reports in local media.
The culture ministry says it dates from the second or 1st Century BC.
Fisherman and free-diver Giacomo De Mola described stumbling across the historic vessel while surveying the seabed near Mazara del Vallo.
He wrote on social media that he had decided to dive and investigate after seeing something that appeared to be a large rock on his scanner.
"I get closer. And my heart stops. It wasn't a rock," he said. Instead, he saw hundreds of amphorae - tall ceramic jars used to store goods in the ancient era, mostly wine, oil or grain.

"This is, without a doubt, the most incredible discovery of my life," he said. "It's hard to describe what it feels like to be among the first humans, in nearly 20 centuries, to see that place again."
He posted a video of the wreck, showing eels, snappers and "countless marine life" living among the jars, noting: "The sea never ceases to amaze us.
"This time we didn't just find a wreck, we found a piece of our history."

items.title: Canadian government steps in as ‘out of control’ wildfires force thousands to flee
body: British Columbia battling 102 fires day and night across province, as breakneck speed hampers firefighters’ efforts

Prefer the Guardian on GoogleCanada’s federal government has announced it will provide urgent assistance to British Columbia after an onslaught of unprecedented fast-moving wildfires that killed one person and forced about 22,000 people to flee their homes in frantic evacuations.

A total of 102 wildfires were raging across the province on Sunday, of which nearly half were categorised as “out of control”, according to the BC Wildfire Service. Of those fires, 78 ignited during the past week.

The entire community of Summerland, about 30 miles (48km) south-west of the city of Kelowna and home to about 12,000 people, was evacuated overnight on Saturday, along with a further 8,000 people around nearby Peachland. About 10,000 others have been told to prepare to evacuate at a moment’s notice.
Anette Boulet was among residents who fled Summerland along Okanagan Lake in British Columbia. As she and her family left around 4.30am Saturday, their home was shrouded in smoke.
“You couldn’t see barely. It was just dark, and the ridge, the ridge of fire just coming towards you,” said Boulet, who evacuated to a centre in Penticton.
“There’s no words to express it, the fear.”

In a social media post on Sunday, Eleanor Olszewski, Canada’s minister of emergency management and community resilience, said she had “approved a request for federal assistance from British Columbia to provide shelter and accommodations for people who have been forced to leave their homes”.
“I have tasked federal officials, led by the government operations centre at Public Safety ‌Canada, to work with the province to ensure support reaches those who need it most,” she ​said.
Efforts to battle the Bald Range wildfire have been hampered by the breakneck speed of its spread.

The blaze was first detected late on Friday evening, and grew within hours to more than 40 sq miles (100 sq km) – nearly twice the size of the island of Manhattan – as it raced nearly nine miles toward Okanagan Lake.

items.title: Spain to introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy
body: Move comes in response to Rome imposing similar measures after mass migration rush to Ceuta

Prefer the Guardian on GoogleSpain has announced it will introduce temporary border checks on visitors from Italy in response to Rome imposing similar measures after a mass rush of people from Morocco into Ceuta.
The checks, which come “amid the persistent irregular migration pressure” facing Italy, will start at midnight on Saturday and last until 7 September, Spain’s interior ministry said in a statement.
Hours earlier, Spain threatened Italy with countermeasures if it did not swiftly lift its own border checks, drawing a rebuff from Rome.
The rare spat between the EU and Nato allies came after tens of thousands of people crossed from Morocco to Spain’s north African territory on 30-31 July in an unprecedented, deadly rush.
The scenes infuriated EU members that back a hard line on irregular immigration, including Italy, which imposed border checks on people arriving from Spain for one month.
Read moreThe Spanish government criticised the measure on Friday as “unfair, contrary to the EU’s interests and discriminatory for the Spanish population”.
Foreign minister José Manuel Albares described it as “a torpedo fired at the hull of European unity”.
“We urge the government of Italy to rectify, put an end to the checks and treat Spaniards like other European citizens,” he added.
He threatened “proportional measures” in response by Sunday if Italy failed to comply.

Within hours, the government of Italy’s far-right prime minister, Giorgia Meloni, said it “had no intention of revising the decision” before 15 August, when it said Spanish authorities “expected a new wave of migration” to hit Ceuta.
